label: Guilt & past mistakes
title: Bhagavad Gita on Guilt & Past Mistakes: 7 Verses
description: Seven verses for something you can't stop replaying: why we do wrong (3.36), the raft across (4.36) and the turn that counts (9.30). Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on guilt and past mistakes: 7 verses
subtitle: For the thing you keep replaying. Read one a day, or all seven tonight.
keywords: bhagavad gita on forgiveness of sins
intro: Arjuna asks a question many of us ask at night: why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to (3.36)? Krishna's answers are some of the most hopeful in the Gita. Even the worst wrongdoer crosses over on the raft of understanding (4.36). Fire turns wood to ash (4.37). Whoever turns around wholeheartedly is counted among the good (9.30). You still owe others whatever amends are due, and these verses free you to make them. The last is from the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira after the war.

days.heading: Why did I do it?
days.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
days.forYou: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
days.today: Write what happened in two sentences, with no adjectives about yourself.

days.heading: The raft across
days.line: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across.
days.forYou: Krishna says even if you were the worst of all wrongdoers, the raft of understanding would carry you across. Guilt says you are what you did. The verse says you can cross over from it, with the river still there behind you.
days.today: Ask yourself: what did I not understand then that I understand now?
days.note: Understanding frees you to change and to make amends to anyone you harmed.

days.heading: As fire turns wood to ash
days.line: As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions.
days.forYou: Real understanding, Krishna says, burns away the hold of past actions the way fire turns wood to ash. The event happened. Its grip on you, the replaying and the shame, is what can burn.
days.today: If there's a letter you'd write to the person you hurt, write it, even if you never send it.

days.heading: Counted among the good
days.line: Even if you've done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly, count yourself among the good.
days.forYou: Api cet su-durācāraḥ: even someone who has done great wrong, once they turn wholeheartedly, is to be counted among the good, because their resolve is now right. Krishna looks at the turn as well as the record.
days.today: Name the turn you're making, in one sentence: from now on, I…
days.note: Turning around includes making amends to anyone you harmed.

days.heading: Soon it becomes who you are
days.line: Such a person soon turns good and finds lasting peace. Mark it: no one devoted to me is ever lost.
days.forYou: Kṣipraṃ bhavati dharmātmā: such a person soon becomes good and finds lasting peace. Krishna even tells Arjuna to declare it boldly. The change starts as a decision and becomes character through what you do next.
days.today: Do one act of repair today: an apology, a correction, or help given where you once took.

days.heading: Then set it down
days.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
days.forYou: Krishna's last counsel in the Gita: take refuge in me; I will free you from every wrong; do not grieve (mā śucaḥ). He says it to a man about to act. Once you've owned what you did and done your part, you're allowed to put the weight down.
days.today: Before sleep, say what you've done to make it right. Then say: I'm putting this down tonight.
days.note: Krishna says this to someone about to act. It lifts fear, and your responsibilities stay with you.

days.heading: He won the war and wanted to disappear

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.body: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.forYou: Running away can feel like the only honest answer to what you did. Yudhishthira's family argue for staying and doing good with what's left.
days.today: Choose one ongoing way to give back that's connected to what happened, and start it this week.

verse.sanskrit: धनञ्जय कृतं पापं कल्याणेनोपहन्यते । ख्यापनेनानुतापेन दानेन तपसाऽपि वा ॥
verse.line: A wrong you did can be outweighed by the good you do next: own it, regret it, give back.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about guilt?
faq.a: Arjuna asks why people do wrong even against their will (3.36). Krishna answers that understanding carries even the worst wrongdoer across like a raft (4.36) and burns away the hold of past actions like fire (4.37), and that whoever turns wholeheartedly is to be counted among the good (9.30).

faq.q: Does the Gita say past mistakes can be forgiven?
faq.a: Yes. In 18.66 Krishna says he will free the one who takes refuge in him from all wrongs, and asks him not to grieve. The Gita pairs this with action: owning what you did and making it right.

faq.q: Which Gita verse helps with regret?
faq.a: 4.36 and 4.37 for the weight of the past, 9.30 and 9.31 for starting again, and 6.5 for not pushing yourself down.
